title: Denisova & Cairns 2019, Player experience and deceptive expectations of difficulty adaptation in digital games, Entertainment Computing 29:56-68
label: research
claim: Two between-subject studies on immersion (IEQ). Study 1 n=120, 2x3 (adaptive timer vs standard timer x no/partial/full information), 1.5-min shooter 'Nightmares': adaptation raised immersion F(1,114)=22.37 p<.001 partial eta2=.164; information raised immersion F(2,114)=5.08 p=.008, and this held whether or not the adaptation was real; no adaptation-by-information interaction. Study 2 n=60, 2x2 (difficulty adaptation of player health/attack and enemy detection radius vs none x told-it-adapts vs not), level-based 'Trick or Treat', two 10-min sessions: both adaptation (F(1,59)=9.49 p=.003 eta2=.145 session 1) and information raised immersion; information effect did not decay after 20 min (H4 rejected). Authors conclude developers need not fear telling players about adaptation 'at least in some circumstances'. Limits stated by authors: study-1 adaptation was a timer not core mechanic, sessions short, repetitive purpose-built games, novelty/pro-innovation bias possible, 'deceptive' framing raises ethics. Self-report immersion only. I read the PDF text extracted with pdftotext; read the abstract, methods headings, results and limitation passages, not every paragraph.

title: Denisova & Cairns 2015, Adaptation in Digital Games: The Effect of Challenge Adjustment on Player Performance and Experience, CHI PLAY
label: research
claim: n=42 (14 women), between-subject; players unaware of the manipulation; timer extended/reduced from performance in a short shooting game ('Nightmares'). Adaptive-timer group was more immersed: one-way ANOVA F(1,40)=7.41 p=0.010. No participant reported noticing the timer change; groups did not differ in perceived challenge. Authors note adaptation 'could be used to improve PX' but the paper says the flow challenge-skill claim 'is only backed up by theoretical literature ... without much empirical evidence'. Tiny task (about 90 s), adaptation was time not difficulty of mechanics. I read the PDF via pdftotext; partial read (intro, abstract, method and results fragments).

title: Constant & Levieux 2019, Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment Impact on Players' Confidence, CHI '19
label: research
claim: Between-subject, three small purpose-built games (logical, motor, sensory), in-game 1-7 bet on own success as the confidence measure. Random-difficulty vs DDA targeting P(success)=0.5. Players underestimate high difficulty (the 'hard effect' = overconfidence) in general; DDA produced larger overestimation of success chances than random difficulty (strongest in motor game, weaker in logical, absent in sensory game where players see part of the task before betting). 138 participants randomly assigned (final n=131 logical, 133 motor, 129 sensory after outlier removal; 76 regular players; median age 15). Gender, self-efficacy, risk aversion, gaming habits did not explain estimation error. Authors state it is only an assumption that overconfidence raises motivation or enjoyment; they did NOT measure enjoyment or motivation; bet system cannot separate effort from skill-based difficulty; simple adaptation only. Read: abstract, discussion, limitations, conclusion from the open HAL PDF.

title: Hades God Mode explained by Supergiant Games (Can I Play That?)
label: developer
claim: Supergiant (tweet) said they wanted to 'open up the thrilling experience of rogue-like games to more players'; Kasavin: God Mode 'reinforces our belief that the way to approach difficulty settings may need to be proprietary to the game.' Mechanic as reported: starts at 20% damage resistance, +2% per death (a WebSearch summary of other outlets gave a cap of 80%; the cap is not verified from this page). The page, read through a summarizing fetch tool, did not state anything about achievements; other outlets disagree on that, unverified. Secondary outlet relaying developer statements.

title: Vice: Celeste assist mode wording change
label: developer
claim: Thorson (Celeste designer; the Vice piece uses an older name and pronoun, the designer is now Maddy Thorson) said the aim was 'to accept that every player is different, and that people come into the game at many different skill levels'; response to Assist Mode 'overwhelmingly positive'. After accessibility critic Clint Lexa said the preamble felt 'othering', the text was changed (from calling difficulty 'essential' to the game being 'intended' to be challenging) and the icon marking save files that used Assist Mode was dropped, because that shaming 'feels like the same exclusionary reasoning'. Read through a summarizing fetch tool, so quotes are as reported by that tool, not checked against the page bytes.

title: Juul, The Art of Failure (book page and TOC, via search)
label: snippet
claim: Book argues the 'paradox of failure': we generally avoid failure, we experience it when playing, yet we seek out games. TOC chapters: paradox of failure and of tragedy, the feeling of failure, designing failure, fictional failure. Only seen in a search summary.

title: Hunicke & Chapman, AI for Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment in Games (Hamlet, Half-Life SDK), AAAI workshop paper
label: research
claim: System paper, not a player study: probabilistic (inventory-theory) DDA that adjusts supply of ammo/health/enemies by estimated player trajectory. Its own Evaluation section says no evaluation has been run yet; it only plans a heart-rate study ('If the adjusted game is able to keep test subjects equally aroused over time, while ... keeping them alive longer, then we will consider the work a success'). Abstract premise 'Video Games are boring when they are too easy and frustrating when they are too hard' is stated, not tested. This is the Hamlet paper; I did not locate the separate 'Case for DDA' ACE 2005 text, so claims about that paper are unverified.

title: Foch & Kirman, 'Slow down and look': Desirable aspects of failure in video games, from the perspective of players (author version)
label: research
claim: Qualitative: online survey of 244 players, reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes for valued failure: opportunity to learn, opportunity for meaningful social interaction, deeply affective experience (anger/frustration followed by pride after overcoming). Self-selected respondents, self-report. Quotes include a Dark Souls fan who values the frustration because overcoming a boss is 'UTTERLY AMAZING'. Authors note failure usually does not feel good (citing Juul) and that failure as scripted/inevitable reduces the pathos vs failure that was avoidable (a participant on XCOM/Crusader Kings).

title: Cuerdo dissertation 2024 (UCSC), 'Challenge Accepted', section 3.2 'Die-r Consequences' (Cuerdo, Mahajan & Melcer, IEEE CoG 2021)
label: research
claim: Between-subject, simple 2D platformer identical except respawn location: start of game (permadeath), start of level, checkpoint, savepoint (player-chosen). N=72. Kruskal-Wallis: autonomy chi2(3)=9.757 p=.021 eta2=.112 (mean ranks: level 36.89, game 42.86, checkpoint 23.86, savepoint 42.39); curiosity chi2(3)=11.230 p=.011 eta2=.134 (35.64, 48.22, 25.14, 37.00). Bonferroni post hoc: permadeath > checkpoint on autonomy p=.037; savepoint > checkpoint autonomy p=.046; permadeath > checkpoint curiosity p=.005. The authors' hypothesis (least autonomy under permadeath) was NOT supported: checkpoint scored worst; they theorise players had no say where they respawned and the placement may feel arbitrary; the permadeath group also died least (mean 25.06) and autonomy fell with more deaths. Theory is the authors' own, untested. 72 participants in four groups is about 18 per cell; one short purpose-built game.

title: Robb & Zhang 2022, Performance-Based DDA and Player Experience in a 2D Digital Game: A Controlled Experiment, Acta Ludologica 5(1)
label: research
claim: n=221, three versions (DDA, constant control, incrementally increasing). DDA group performed significantly better; 'there were no significant differences in terms of enjoyment or experience of flow'. Only the abstract page was read; effect sizes, disclosure and limits not seen.

title: Aalto master's thesis: DDA in single-player games, player perception on hidden vs upfront DDA
label: snippet
claim: Search summary only: players told about DDA beforehand rated the game 15% more challenging than unaware players (A/B test). Thesis, not peer reviewed; page returned 403, so n and conditions unseen.

title: Last of Us Part II accessibility coverage (Can I Play That, GameSpot, The Gamer, relaying Naughty Dog interviews)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary of developer statements: 'Accessibility is orthogonal to difficulty' (Matthew Gallant, Naughty Dog); options can be changed at any time without penalty, nothing gated behind a difficulty; options not tied to a lower difficulty; several accessibility options began as existing debug-menu switches; granular so players tune to their needs; more than 60 settings per the PlayStation accessibility page. Never opened the articles; job titles differ between outlets.

title: Abuhamdeh & Csikszentmihalyi 2012, Importance of Challenge for the Enjoyment of Intrinsically Motivated, Goal-Directed Activities, PSPB
label: snippet
claim: Search summary of abstract: internet chess (Study 1) and experience sampling (Study 2). Perceived challenge predicted enjoyment; games vs stronger opponents and close games were more enjoyable than vs weaker opponents and blowouts; relation moderated by activity motivation and type. Earlier 2009 work by same authors reports an inverted-U between relative skill (Elo) and enjoyment. Not opened; the shape of the curve and numbers unverified.

title: Automaton: developers wonder about the term 'Easy Mode' (informal poll)
label: opinion
claim: Search summary: a developer's Twitter poll reported 90% said 'Easy Mode' did not give them a bad feeling, but the poll could not reach players likely to play on Easy. A search summary said The First Berserker's developer reported most players hit the exit menu faster than they toggled to Easy, suggesting stigma (second-hand, unverified). Forum posts split on whether assist options cheapen achievements; no formal study found.

title: Vice: Celeste Assist Mode (Thorson statements)
label: developer
claim: Thorson (as quoted by Vice, via summarizing fetch tool): 'We also accept that every player is different, and that people come into the game at many different skill levels.' 'Assist Mode breaks the game.' 'But ultimately, we want to empower the player and give them a good experience, and sometimes that means letting go.' 'The goal is a fluid experience where players are safe to float around between loosely-defined difficulty levels'. Options named by the article: game speed, stamina, number of air dashes, ability to die. The article does NOT contain the 'betrayal' remark.

title: Edge magazine 'Time Extend' on Celeste (via search summary)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary attributes to Thorson: she was 'the team member who was most against' Assist Mode, 'It felt like a betrayal of the precious experience I was designing'; the mode was also cheaper than a difficulty select, which would mean retuning and retesting every level per tier; the original working name was 'Cheat Mode', dropped as 'judgmental'. Unopened; treat as unverified until read.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines full list (titles only)
label: guideline
claim: Titles seen via summarizing fetch (no descriptions): Basic tier: 'Offer a wide choice of difficulty levels'; 'Include an option to adjust the game speed' (motor); 'Ensure that all settings are saved/remembered'. Intermediate: 'Allow difficulty level to be altered during gameplay, either through settings or adaptive difficulty'; 'Include assist modes such as auto-aim and assisted steering'; 'Offer a means to bypass gameplay elements that aren't part of the core mechanic'; 'Provide an autosave feature'; 'Provide a manual save feature'. Advanced: 'Do not make precise timing essential to gameplay - offer alternatives...'. A guideline list, not evidence about enjoyment.

title: Lora Ariza et al., Measuring Control to Dynamically Induce Flow in Tetris (unfinished preprint, abstract reads 'TODO: VOLVER A ESCRIBIR')
label: research
claim: 40 volunteers (18-42, mean age 27.3), repeated-measures over three Tetris versions (trivial, balanced via DDA, normal), Short Flow State Scale. Flow significantly higher in balanced than normal; NO significant difference between trivial and balanced overall (only the autotelic dimension was higher in balanced); authors rejected their own hypothesis that a trivial game would not produce flow. Preprint with a draft abstract, not peer-reviewed as far as seen; custom Tetris where 'trivial' hands the player the best pieces; no exact test statistics read.

title: University of Rochester press release on Przybylski, Deci, Rigby & Ryan, J. Personality and Social Psychology (frustration, competence, aggression)
label: research
claim: Press release for six lab experiments with about 600 college-aged participants plus a survey of 300 avid gamers. Failure to master a game's controls or difficulty drove frustration and hostility irrespective of violent content; a hard Tetris version produced about 10 s more cold-water 'pain' assigned to later participants than an easy one; survey: inability to master game or controls caused frustration and reduced enjoyment. Secondary press release; effect sizes and exact measures unseen. Outcome is aggression, not enjoyment-in-play.

title: Search summaries on Super Meat Boy instant respawn (Wikipedia, GamesBeat, reviews)
label: snippet
claim: Sources agree the level restarts immediately on death in Super Meat Boy; one review argues the speed leaves little time to reflect on mistakes. I found no primary statement from McMillen or Refenes explaining the choice, and no study isolating retry delay.

title: Springer chapter on a taxonomy of death mechanics (Cuerdo & Melcer; via search summary)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary: death is central to how players judge difficulty; frequent deaths in some hard games draw 'unfair' complaints; repetitive deaths 'have been found to increasingly reduce player enjoyment'. Cited source of that last claim not seen.

title: Null search: controlled study of telegraphing or attack readability on perceived fairness
label: snippet
claim: One search specifically for a study of telegraphing or readability against perceived unfairness returned only practitioner articles and the death-mechanics work; no controlled study found. Not proof none exists.

title: Null search: formal study of whether assist options cheapen others' achievement
label: snippet
claim: One search found forum posts and informal polls only (opinions split); no academic survey found.
